notes.1.43: 1.43–44 end a stanza begun in the context: the bold receiver of the 'steed of the fair wind' (a ship), i.e. the ruler, draws under himself with true words the pine-haired waiting-wife of Thridi (Odin), that is Earth: he wins the land. biꝼkvan is read as biðkván, 'waiting-wife'. Hroptatyr and Ygg are names of Odin. 1.51–54 are obscure: the land-holder (the ruler) seems to reward with a headband the 'shaper of the gods' fjord' (poetry), i.e. the poet; hunn, taken as 'mast-head', is unexplained. 1.55–58 are also obscure: the waterfall of horns of the cargo of Gunnlod's arms (Odin, whom Gunnlod held) is the mead of poetry; hlitstyggr, 'averse to enough', seems to describe a generous lord.
notes.1.768: Holgi's mound-thatch is gold (his grave-mound was said to be laid with gold and silver). The six kennings in 1.772–777 are all for gold: Fenja ground gold at the mill; Fafnir's 'Midgard' is his gold-bed; Glasir is the grove with golden leaves; Grani carried Sigurd's gold; the ring Draupnir dripped gold rings; Grafvitnir is a serpent, and serpents lie on gold.
notes.1.549: The 'gnawer of carrion' is the giant Thiazi in eagle form; he is also 'Hymir's kin-tree'. The wolf's father, Thor's confidant, Lopt, the mover of hosts and Brising's girdle-thief are Loki. The maid who knew the Aesir's cure for old age, the lady of Brunnakr's brook, is Idunn. The stone-Nidad is a giant, so his courts are the giants' world. sorg-æyra (1.557) is uncertain, and may describe Loki or the maid.
notes.1.180: 1.181 repeats 1.180 with 'to send' before it; the close of that stanza is uncertain (seinfyrnd, 'slow to age', is taken as describing a lasting poem). Vidrir and Ygg are Odin. Thor is Vidrir's heir, the son of Earth, Magni's father, the father of Thrud, Sif's confidant, Ull's stepfather, the terrifier of Oflugbardi (a giant) and the prince of Bilskirnir (his hall); Roskva's brother is Thjalfi. The World Serpent (Jormungand) is the encircler of all lands, the ring of the steep road, the saithe of the broad earth, the end-saithe of all lands, the fish of the ground and the ugly ring of the road. Eynefir's ski and Roin's ship are ships; the dwelling of the fish is the sea; the stone of strength is the heart; the old man is the giant Hymir; the bane of the gorge-whale (a giant) is Thor's hammer. 'The horn-stream gotten from Hrimnir' may be the poem itself. 1.198–199, 1.200 (ſẏioꝛ, perhaps the boat's strakes) and 1.208–209 do not construe with certainty. In 1.200–203 renndi is the transitive 'drove': the serpent's pull drives the boat's strakes (or their rivets) out at the gunwale, so the boat is breaking.
notes.1.81: 1.81–82 end an obscure stanza begun in the context: to bail the bilge of a god's ships seems to mean pouring out poetry, here before a warrior (the 'arrow-speeder'); Vingnad is not identified. The Raven-tester is Odin, and the fallen son, for whom Heimdall rides to the pyre, is Baldr.
notes.1.120: 1.120 ends a stanza from the context and does not construe on its own. Kvasir's blood is poetry, and so is 'the surf of the dregs of the men of the fjord-bone': the fjord-bone is rock, its men are dwarves, and their drink is the mead of poetry. ꝺreggíat (1.124) is read as dreggjar.
notes.1.258: Grjotbjorn, 'stone-bear', is probably a play on the name Arinbjorn (arinn, 'hearth-stone'). 1.262 begins a new stanza; ræstr is unclear.
notes.1.25: 1.25–26 end a stanza begun in the context. Atal's beasts are ships; the 'victory-god' of the ships may be the sea-warrior himself, or Odin present in the 'attacking elf' (the warrior); the construction is uncertain. Gautatyr is a name of Odin; Gondul and Skogul are valkyries.
notes.1.137: Odin's mead is poetry. hapta beiðir, 'ruler of the gods' (hapt, 'fetters', is a name for the gods), is Odin; the line runs on beyond the unit.
notes.1.343: Lopt, 'the father of the fire-thread' (the Serpent, his son), is Loki, here goading Thor to leave home. The two kennings in 1.343–344 are obscure, and which god each names is uncertain. The 'tester of minds' is probably Loki again. 1.343–346 in prose order: the father of the fire-thread (Loki) set about urging from home the feller of the life-net of the gods of the flight-ledges (Thor, killer of giants); Lopt was great at lying.
notes.1.498: The poet describes a scene painted on a shield ('Hild's lid', if vez is so read; Hild is a valkyrie): the risky journey of three gods and the giant Thiazi. The 'lady's wolf' is Thiazi, the ravisher of Idunn, flying in eagle form.
notes.1.523: The giant Thiazi, in eagle form, settles where the gods are cooking an ox. The 'lord of the land' is probably Thiazi; Farbauti's son is Loki; the 'whale of the clatter-rope' seems to be the ox. vara (1.526) is unexplained.
notes.1.539: The burden of Sigyn's arms is Loki, her husband; the fosterer of the ski-god (probably Skadi) is her father, the giant Thiazi. The reference of 'war-booty' (1.539) is uncertain; æẏgía (1.542) is read as 'look upon'.
